input:
This note sets out a capital appraisal for a proposed new bottling line and reaches a clear conclusion: on the figures currently available, the investment is financially attractive, with a net present value of $516k at a discount rate of 10%, the present value of the expected savings being $1850k when set against an installed cost of $1334k.

The savings in question are put at $301k per year for 10 years, and it is the discounting of that stream of savings at the company's discount rate that produces the present value quoted above, the difference between that present value and the installed cost being, by definition, the net present value of the project.

A word of caution is nevertheless in order. The savings figures are not based on any measured performance: they are estimates provided by the vendor and by the utility, and no saving has as yet been measured on a comparable installation anywhere. The appraisal therefore stands or falls with the quality of those estimates, and should the savings actually achieved fall persistently short of the estimate, the net present value would fall correspondingly, a possibility that the appraisal itself does nothing to exclude. The recommendation to proceed accordingly rests on the estimates as they stand, and the first hard evidence will come from savings actually measured on a comparable line.
target:
The bottling line clears its appraisal. The net present value is $516k at a discount rate of 10%: the present value of the expected savings is $1850k, against an installed cost of $1334k.

The appraisal compares two amounts at one date: the cost falls at installation, and the savings arrive over the operating life that follows it. Discounting puts the later savings on the same footing as the present cost, and the surplus of the one amount over the other is the measure on which the decision rests.

The savings behind the appraisal are $301k per year for 10 years, discounted at the stated rate to the present value in the opening. The margin between the present value of the savings and the installed cost is the net present value, and it is positive on the figures as supplied.

The result rests on estimates, not measurements. The savings are vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so the evidence base for the finding is the estimates as supplied rather than operating data. A measured saving persistently below the estimate would reduce the net present value, and nothing in the appraisal rules that out. The appraisal supports proceeding on the estimates, and the first measured savings on a comparable line are the evidence that would confirm or overturn it.
